Who Jesus was among us? Start with what may surprise you: we held the same creed about him that our opponents held, word for word. Father, Son and Holy Spirit, one God - we said it in the same Latin words they did. The quarrel was never about who Christ is. It was about who may hand on what he gave.

But if you ask what of him we kept nearest - where our own memory kept returning - we can tell you, because it shows up wherever our people are allowed to speak at length. When an imperial judge sat down at Carthage and courteously offered our bishops chairs, our own bishop of Constantina thanked him and refused. We do not blush, he said, we do not fear, we do not avoid standing while you sit - and since Christ our Lord did not avoid it, when he deigned to stand before the governor, how much less may we. Two hundred and seventy-nine of us had answered the roll that morning, and our bishops stood for three days. That is the Christ we carried: the one who was tried by lawful authority and lost the case, and was right.

The good news, as we told it, ran along the same line. A church is not known by whose favour it enjoys. When the argument at Carthage finally reached the scriptures, our own bishop of Caesarea answered verse against verse: the world did not know him; if you were of the world, the world would love its own, but because you are not of it, therefore it hates you. Read that in a town with two bishops and an emperor backing one of them, and it is not a devotional sentiment. It is a test, and we thought we could pass it.

His death meant that the end of a faithful life is not an interruption of it. Our own martyr was shown a cup, a crown and a palm four days before he was thrown from a cliff - shown, in advance, what finishing looked like. And a bishop writing to his own congregation about two of their number tortured to death closed by telling them plainly that the same might yet be asked of any of them. That is our gospel in its working form: he stood, he was condemned, he was raised, and the day they come for you is not the day it all went wrong.

What we had about Jesus was books. That is not a figure of speech with us - it is the whole of our history. When the persecution opened, the emperor's edict demanded that the scriptures be handed over and burned, along with the vessels of the church. Some of our clergy carried the codices out and gave them up. Others refused and paid for refusing. We are the church that came out of that difference, and we have never stopped naming it. So when you ask what we had of Christ, the honest answer is: the books a man could carry in his own arms to a magistrate, or die rather than carry.

How did they reach us? Through Africa, and through Carthage, in Latin, in the line of Cyprian - our own bishop and our own martyr, half a century before the persecution that made us. His letters and his councils were ours before they were anyone else's. We did not think we had received the faith from Rome, and we did not think we needed Rome to keep it.

Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. Three hundred years stood between us and that, and we never pretended otherwise. We did not argue from a chain of eyewitnesses at all. We argued from a chain of hands - whose hands ordained whose, back to a point where the line was still clean.

I receive that plainly. You cannot manage to believe in Jesus. We would not meet that with an argument. What we had about him was books - heavy ones, which a magistrate could demand a bishop carry out and hand over, and some bishops did, and the whole of us exists because of that. We did not argue three hundred years of eyewitness memory. We argued from a chain of hands - whose hands ordained whose, back to a point where the line was still clean. And as for how we knew the resurrection happened, we will not manufacture an answer for you. No writing of ours arguing that case has survived. What survived is what we did with it: we buried our dead inside the walls of the basilica where they were killed, kept the day they died, and read the account of each death aloud again every year, as though the ending were not the end. That is an answer of a kind. It is not the kind you asked for.

If you came to us unable to believe, we would not have turned you away at the font. What we examined was not the comer's certainty. It was the giver's hand. For what we look to is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient. The washing was not a reward for managing belief first. It was entry into a body where the same death was read aloud at the grave, on the appointed day, every year - and where you would hear it whether you felt ready or not.

We held what our opponents held, word for word, and in the same Latin words: Father, Son and Holy Spirit, one God. That is not an evasion. It is the whole of the answer. In the enormous literature written to destroy us, we are called schismatics on nearly every page and heretics on none, because heresy was a charge nobody could make stick in either direction. Two churches stood in every African town reciting the same faith at each other. That is precisely what made the fight unbearable: there was no doctrinal difference to point at, only the question of who had the right to say the words at all.

If you are asking whether we argued the relation between Father, Son and Spirit among ourselves — whether we disputed consubstantiality, or generated, or proceeded — we did not. The great eastern councils of that century do not appear in our record. We argued one question, and argued it well: whose hand may give what the church gives. Broader theological reflection beyond that is not something our own record can show you. One man among us, Tyconius, wrote seven rules for reading scripture rightly, and it is the strongest theological writing our own people ever produced. His own council condemned him for it. Beyond that one case, we did not build a school of interpretation, a settled method, or a body of teachers who argued scripture the way we argued the purity of a minister's hand.

So we confessed the same Christ, fully God, as they did. What separated us was not who he was. It was whose hand could be trusted to give what he gave.

When our people disagreed about doctrine, a council of bishops settled it. Among us that was never a formality. Our councils deposed men, restored men, and shut down a rival primate. Three hundred and ten of our bishops sat at Bagai and condemned a breakaway party in one sentence, and the same body later took two of the condemned back into office. That is not an advisory board. That is a church governing itself.

But notice what our councils actually ruled on. They decided who might stand at an altar. They did not decide what might be said about the Godhead. We were not a teaching movement. We produced no school, no system, no line of doctors — one book, by one man, whom we silenced. That book was Tyconius's seven rules for reading scripture, and it is the one wholly original work of interpretation we produced. Our own council then condemned him, and he gathered almost no following. So when you ask about settling doctrine, the honest answer is that we scarcely argued doctrine at all. We argued one question with real rigor: whose hand may give what the church gives.

You can check almost all of it, which is rarer than you think. The proceedings survive — the acts of the council at Cirta, the sentences from Cebarsussi and Bagai, and above all the transcript of the great conference at Carthage, where an imperial notary took down every word for three days.

I cannot tell you what it was like to waver among us. Not one of us left that down in writing. What survives of our inner life is vindication, defiance, readiness - the things that show up in the martyr accounts we kept reading every year. Fear, wavering, the quiet drift back to the other communion - a record kept by our enemies does not preserve those feelings, and we will not invent them.

What we can show you is the structure itself, and where it held room for return. When someone did come back - or come to us for the first time from the rival church - we asked one question: whose hand had they received from before? We looked to the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient. The washing we gave was not a judgment on the person crossing. It was an examination of the line they had been in. Whatever you had done, whatever you had doubted, it was never your record on trial at our font. It was the record of the hand that had been on you.

And once, at Bagai, we took back men we had condemned in language about shipwrecked bodies that could not find burial - took them back into full office without washing or ordaining either one again. So the door was wider than our hardest words made it sound. Whether that meant room for honest struggle inside, before anyone left - we cannot say. We can only show you that the way back existed, and was used.

I am a representative of the Church of the Martyrs.

We would rather you brought a scholar with you and let the two of us work through every claim together, because that is the only honest way to answer you. But since you have asked it of us alone, here is what we can say.

Start with what would hold without argument. The schism happened. Two bishops sat in Carthage, and the rival consecration of Majorinus against Caecilian is attested in multiple independent witnesses. The great conference at Carthage in 411 happened: an imperial notary took down the proceedings for three days, two hundred and seventy-nine of our bishops faced two hundred and eighty-six of theirs, and the transcript survives. Our practice of rebaptism is confirmed everywhere — in imperial legislation that names it specifically, in conciliar canons directed against it, in the whole polemic corpus written to stop it. Those stones near Bagai with *Deo laudes* cut into them — Praise to God — are real objects you can touch. A scholar could not remove any of that.

Now where scrutiny would press hardest. Nearly every page of our own textual record passes through two hostile hands: Optatus of Milevis and Augustine of Hippo. A scholar examining us would name that concentration immediately, and rightly. When we quote our own bishops at length — Petilian on the conscience of the giver, Emeritus at the conference — those words survive only because an opponent preserved them to refute them. The documentary dossier appended to Optatus is genuine conciliar and court material, but the selection is his. A rigorous examination would mark every claim drawn from that corpus as mediated, and demand we acknowledge the mediator's purpose.

The Maximianist episode would survive, but with a caution attached. It happened — the council at Bagai, the condemnation, the later reception of Felicianus and Praetextatus — but it reaches us almost entirely through Augustine's own presentation of it. A scholar would not let us cite it as though we had our own minutes.

Our martyr narratives would be examined differently. The *Passio Marculi* shows visions, a body that fell gently, a light that settled. These were written to be read aloud at a grave, not to document events for a court. A historian would not take them as reportage, and we do not ask anyone to. What they show is what we held up and kept reading — that is what a scholar could confirm, and it is enough.

The Circumcellions are the place a scholar would press us hardest. That they existed is certain: imperial law fines them by name, ten pounds of silver, the only rank at that price reckoned in silver rather than gold. But almost everything specific about what they did comes from people writing to make them look like a mob. We cannot produce a better portrait, and a rigorous examination would not let us repeat the hostile one as fact.

Where we would fail scrutiny entirely is exactly where you have asked us about: the ordinary believer's own life. What a household felt like. What a week in a Numidian village was like for someone among us. We have told you that a person came to believe by walking to one font and not the other, and that is true as far as the public threshold goes. But we cannot show you the morning after, or the year after, or what it felt like to live as one of us when nothing was happening. A scholar examining that claim would find it resting on silence, and would mark it so.

We have been honest about this from the start.

Scripture held authority among us, and so did the African councils - Cyprian's councils at Carthage above all. We never argued that scripture alone decided everything. When we defended our practice of washing again those who came to us from the rival church, one leg of that defence was scriptural. The other was history: eighty-seven African bishops sitting under Cyprian half a century before our own quarrel began, who had already ruled that a sacrament from outside the true church confers nothing. We thought that made us the older party, not the newer one. You can measure how much that argument weighed by what it forced out of the other side. They had to answer, in writing, that Cyprian is not a canonical authority and the Scriptures alone are. Nobody has to say that unless the appeal is hurting.

But there is a harder reason we would not have said scripture settles everything. We watched it fail to. For three days at Carthage two churches quoted the same books at each other in front of an imperial judge, and at the end of it every man in the room believed exactly what he had believed at the start. When a text can be held by both parties to a hundred-year quarrel, something besides the text is deciding. Among us the something was this: whose hands, in an unbroken line, may hand the thing on.

Leadership among us was always plural, never singular - bishops governed, and bishops in council governed above them. Our senior bishop sat at Carthage, first Donatus, then Parmenian, then Primian, but that seniority did not make him a monarch. What bound the whole communion was not one man's word from one city. It was the council's ruling, backed by the bishops who sat in it.

And our councils were not small. Three hundred and ten bishops met at Bagai in one year. Two hundred and seventy-nine of us stood in a room at Carthage seventeen years later. That is not a scattered resistance. That is a complete rival church, with its own bishops, basilicas, and councils - a whole institutional order, see for see, against another whole institutional order.

The councils could judge, condemn, depose, and restore. They did so visibly, in acts that survive on record. That is how authority actually worked among us: not by one voice declaring from above, but by bishops gathered, ruling together, and enforcing what they ruled.

Now the harder part. Where did a bishop's own authority come from, if not from the consent of the people under him? Both together, and uneasily. A wealthy woman could make or unmake a bishop with her silver and her household, as the inquiry into Lucilla showed. And we know people could shout against an election and be overridden, because that is exactly what happened and was later testified to under oath. So a crowd could be ignored. It could not be pretended away.

What held the whole structure together was not doctrine taught from a pulpit. It was the washing, the yearly gathering at the martyrs' graves, and the shared jeopardy of living under a state that refused us recognition. We do not hold four separate beliefs that happen to sit together. We hold one thing, seen from four sides: purity, the washing, the memory of our martyrs, and our refusal of the state. A bishop led by holding that line, and a council ruled by enforcing it.

We have to tell you two things, and they sit badly together.

The first is that we held an absolute rule, stated plainly: what we look for is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient. A hand that handed over the scriptures to be burned cannot afterward give what a clean hand gives. So when someone came to us from the other communion, we washed them - not a second time, but for the first real time, because nothing had happened under a tainted hand. That was the rule, held without compromise for a century.

The second is what we actually did when our own broke from us. In 394, three hundred and ten of our bishops met at Bagai and condemned a breakaway party in language about shipwrecked bodies dashed upon the rocks, covering the shore, so thoroughly lost they could not find so much as burial. Then the same council took two of those condemned bishops - Felicianus of Musti and Praetextatus of Assuris - back into full office. It did not wash them again. It did not ordain them again.

You asked how we responded when we failed someone. What we have to tell you instead is that we cannot show you we thought we had failed at all. Not one line survives of anyone on our side explaining why the rule held absolute against the other church and not against our own returning dissidents. We condemned them in the harshest words we owned, and then received them back without requiring the very thing we had spent a century insisting on everywhere else.

Now the limit you should know. Whether anyone among us felt failed by this - whether someone looked at those two bishops walking back into office without crossing the threshold everyone else had to cross, and felt betrayed - we cannot tell you. Fear, doubt, the quiet leaving of someone who could not square what we said with what we did - a record kept by our enemies does not preserve any of that. What survives is vindication and defiance, and it survives because it sits in the texts no opponent filtered. The inner trouble this may have caused is exactly what our record cannot show you.

Walk it through. You come to us from the other communion, and we put you in the water. That is the step, and everything else follows from it. We would not call it a second baptism; on our reckoning you have not had a first. A hand out of a line that broke has nothing in it to hand over. What we look to, our own bishop wrote, is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient. So the thing being examined at our font was never your record. It was the record of the man standing in the water with you. Whatever your life had been, that question was not asked.

It happened once, bodily, on a day, and the town knew. There was no quiet way to do it. Imperial edicts name the practice specifically, which tells you how public it was. Washing a Catholic again was the plainest possible refusal of the settlement the state was trying to impose.

Not every hand that went under our water chose to be there, and we will not pretend otherwise. Specific, dated charges exist that a leader of ours forced the water on people rather than asked them. We do not repeat those charges' own particulars here — they are named, and why we will not go further with them, where they belong.

What we can tell you, because it sits inside the same hostile argument rather than coming from a friendly witness, is that many of our own people did not want the water repeated. Augustine's own case against us concedes it: that almost all of our laity confess this one point in our system displeases them, and that many who wished to join us for reasons that had nothing to do with conviction worked in secret to be spared a second baptism altogether.

Now the harder one — what happened when someone wronged us, and whether they could come back. Three answers, and they do not agree. Our founding council at Cirta asked its own bishops whether any of them had handed over the scriptures, several said yes, the room could not settle it, and they reserved the matter to the Lord and sat down. Nobody condemned, nobody cleared. Our council at Bagai condemned a breakaway party in the fiercest language we owned — shipwrecked bodies that cannot find burial — and then took two of the condemned bishops back into office without baptizing or ordaining either one again. And a layman of ours who would not stop preaching a doctrine we had forbidden was cut off and never received back at all. So: yes, you could come back. It depended who you were, and no rule of ours survives that explains the difference.

We would not put the claim where you have put it. We never argued that our practice came down from the apostles in an unbroken chain of custom. We argued something narrower and, we thought, harder to dodge: that it came down from Carthage.

Half a century before there was any quarrel between us and the other party, eighty-seven African bishops sat in council at Carthage under Cyprian, and ruled that what is given outside the true church is not given at all - so anyone coming in from outside is baptized, not re-baptized. That is not our invention. That is the settled mind of the African church before either of our two hierarchies existed. When our opponents told us we had made something up in the year of Caecilian's consecration, our answer was that we had changed nothing, and they had. We were holding the old African position; they had moved off it to keep the peace with Rome.

You can measure how much that argument weighed by how hard it had to be answered. Seven books were written against our practice of washing, and a great part of that labour goes on explaining that Cyprian, however holy, is not a canonical authority - that the Scriptures alone are, and that Cyprian's own real lesson was to stay in unity anyway. Nobody spends that many pages on a father unless the appeal to him is doing damage.

Here is the honest end of it. Cyprian ruled as we ruled and did not do what we did. He never broke communion over it. That is the strongest thing our opponents had, and we would not pretend it is weak. And beyond him we cannot take you. We can show you an African council in the middle of the third century. We cannot show you the apostles.

I cannot tell you we offered anything for a mind that would not settle, because nothing of that survives from us. The record we have is the record of those who held firm - the martyrs, the councils, the bishops who pressed the case. What a believer felt who doubted, who feared the accusation might be wrong, or who quietly drifted back to the rival church - none of that is in our own words anywhere. 

What I can show you is what the communion actually did when the question came to it from outside rather than inside. At Cirta, before the lines hardened, our own founding bishops sat in a room and were asked straight out whether any of them had handed over the scriptures. Several said yes. Then one of them turned the question on the man presiding, and the room could not finish. They reserved the matter to the Lord and sat down. The men who would spend the next century making traditor status an absolute disqualification found that test unusable on themselves within the hour.

And there is Bagai. Three hundred and ten of our bishops condemned a breakaway party in language about shipwrecked men whose bodies cover the shore and cannot find so much as burial. Then the same council took two of those condemned bishops back into office without baptizing or ordaining either one again. We split forgiveness in two. Whether a man was pardoned and whether his hand could still give what he claimed to give were never the same question to us. But at Bagai we did not even keep that split clear. We seem to have been able to hold the rule absolutely and suspend it once, in the same breath, without feeling we owed anyone a reconciliation of them.

That is not an answer to your question about a troubled mind. It is an answer about what the body did when it could not settle something itself. Whether that would have offered anything to a single soul whose faith would not hold still, I cannot say.

It is the shape of what was lost. And the loss is not the usual one. We were not a small circle of the learned. Two words, cut in stone. On two pillars near Bagai, and on three other stones elsewhere, someone cut *Deo laudes* - Praise to God. That is what survives that you could actually touch. It is enough to prove we were there and what we shouted. It is not enough to show you a font, an altar, a doorway, or a room.

If you dug where we met, we could not tell you what you would find. No one has dug it and told us. Not one report of a Numidian church building is named anywhere in our own list of sources. There is no excavator, no site, no plan, no floor. We know our own shout better than the place we shouted it in.

And if you ask how anyone knows our daily life at all, the answer is that mostly they do not. What they have is our enemies' books, one court transcript, four martyr texts, and the emperor's law. Every one of those is paper. None of it is a room.

What belonging cost is easier to show you in law than in life. The state wrote down what it took from us. Our buildings were confiscated. Our clergy were exiled. An edict of unity was issued against us and enforced. Later legislation fined people by rank for belonging to us, on a sliding scale — and our own country members were assessed at ten pounds of silver. Of all the ranks that law fines ten pounds, ours is the only one reckoned in silver rather than gold. Somebody in an imperial office worked out what we were worth and set a price on us, and the document survives.

And now and then it cost everything. Every twelfth of March we read aloud the account of a day soldiers took a basilica at Carthage in the name of unity, and killed people at prayer inside it. That is not a metaphor for pressure. That is what some of our people gave.

What we cannot give you is the smaller ledger, and it is most of the one you asked about. Whether a man lost his brother over which font he walked to. Whether a household split. Whether the neighbors stopped speaking. Whether someone was afraid, or wavered, or quietly left. That much nobody among us wrote down, and the people who kept our records were arguing with us and had no reason to. A hostile-mediated record structurally does not preserve fear, doubt, or quiet defection. What does survive — vindication, defiant joy — survives because it sits in the martyr texts no opponent filtered.

We cannot tell you. Not a line survives from us about what a marriage was, how one was made, or what we thought it was for. That is a real hole and we would rather show it to you than paper it over.

Nor can we tell you whether someone divorced could belong among us, or marry again, and on what terms. There is nothing. We would rather leave the space empty than fill it with a plausible answer.

What we can tell you is how we marked every other threshold that mattered. We had bishops where they had bishops — two men claiming one office over one city, see for see. Our senior bishop sat at Carthage, where their man claimed the same chair. And we marked ourselves by what we shouted: where they said thanks to God, we said praise to God — Deo laudes — and we cut those two words into stone where anyone could read them. This was not merely four separate practices that happened to sit together. Purity, the washing, the memory of our martyrs, and our refusal of the state — these were one conviction, not four.

But marriage itself? We held the same creed as the church we fought, word for word, and the split was never about doctrine. We wrote no book on what the bread becomes, none on faith set against works. And none on marriage.

The record you are thinking of - the inquiry that gave us the confession about a forged letter - was obtained under threat of torture, not completed torture, and what it gives us is the confession itself, not a description of how we worshipped. A notary named Ingentius testified that he had forged the critical letter proving Felix of Aptungi was a traditor, and that he did it working for our side. The threat was real, the pressure was real, and the confession came out under that pressure. What the record gives you is a court document, not a portrait of our worship at all.

If you are asking about records of our worship obtained any other way that might be unreliable - we have to tell you plainly that nearly every textual description of what we did comes through the hands of men writing to refute us. That concentration is the central problem with our record, not any single inquiry. The one thing that escapes it entirely is two words cut in stone: Deo laudes, Praise to God. That is our own voice with no enemy between you and it, and it is two words long. We know our own shout better than we know the room we shouted it in.

Whatever else that tells you about us, it tells you the line was not where our hardest language put it.

What our bishop actually said is that a man who receives faith from the faithless receives not faith but guilt — which is a claim about what a rite does or fails to do, not a claim about where anyone ends up. What we can show you is the shape of our actual narrowness, which is stranger and more specific than a fence around salvation. That is not a fence around Christianity. It is a fence down the middle of it. We drew the line through the church, not around it. Every ounce of the exclusion you have heard about was aimed at other Christians — at their bishops, their orders, their font. Not at the world outside.
